definition.text: A microclimate is the local set of air, soil and water conditions near the ground that differs measurably from the surrounding area.

facts.text: A microclimate can be anything from a few meters to at most a few kilometers across.
Climate is described at nested scales: macroclimates span hundreds to thousands of kilometers, mesoclimates tens to hundreds, and microclimates far less.
Microclimates are shaped by terrain, soil, vegetation, water and human-made features, which change sunlight, wind, heat and moisture near the surface.
A wooded park stays different from a nearby industrial park because leaves absorb light and heat that roofs and parking lots radiate back into the air.
Farmers manage microclimates with irrigation, shading, windbreaks and vegetation to buffer crops from heat and drought, which matters more as climate extremes grow.
A clearing wider than twice the height of nearby trees loses the woodland's moderating effect on the microclimate.
Habitat fragmentation can change microclimates locally and regionally, affecting biodiversity.

definition.text: A nursery habitat is a place where young marine animals live that contributes more young to the adult population per unit area than other places they use.

facts.text: Mangroves, salt marshes and seagrass are typical nursery habitats for many marine species.
Seagrass meadows give nursery habitat to over a fifth of the world's 25 largest fisheries, including walleye pollock, the most landed species.
Losing nursery habitats can mean fewer young reaching adulthood, shrinking populations needed for both biodiversity and fishing.
Juvenile density alone is not enough evidence; the best measure is how much biomass moves from juvenile to adult populations.

definition.text: Pollination management is the farming practice of ensuring or improving a crop's pollination by managing pollinators, pollen-supplying plants and conditions.

facts.text: Besides honey bees, growers use blue orchard bees, bumblebees, hand pollination and even machines.
Too few pollinators can limit yield, called pollination limitation; it fell by 50% between 1950 and the 2010s, mainly because fields were supplied with managed pollinators.
Bigger monoculture fields make management more important; the blue orchard bee visits only the target tree and is 100 times more efficient per bee than a honeybee.
A 1950s grower of ten acres of watermelons had wild bees enough, but today's 200-acre grower must bring hives to the field.
